body:
This is a very, very wacky movie and I mean that as both praise and warning.

Gore Verbinski throws a ton of satirical, very current ideas into a meat grinder and intentionally spits them back out, hoping something sticks. A lot of it actually does. The movie is extremely on-the-nose with its messaging, but it's also integral to the plot, and Verbinski makes some genuinely interesting choices with how those ideas are deployed rather than just stated.

The film splits into multiple character storylines, though this approach isn't nearly as effective as what Weapons pulled off last year. Still, those threads do expand the world and shed light on a setting that's undeniably wild and unique. Some moments are so chaotic they're hard to fully process even in hindsight but I'll give it this, it's memorable in a way most studio movies aren't anymore.

Sam Rockwell is the unhinged, funny, and occasionally serious rock at the center of it all. He's clearly having a blast, and the movie leans on him hard. Other performances don't quite land the same way, but that feels intentional. This isn't a movie chasing emotional depth so much as it is throwing characters into absurd situations and seeing how they survive them.

My biggest gripe is the R-rating. It feels like the movie wanted to go harder with the violence but couldn't quite decide if it wanted to be lighthearted and darkly funny or fully commit to something more brutal. That hesitation holds it back a bit.

Messy, loud, uneven but also creative, strange, and hard to forget. Honestly, I'll take that over safe any day.

The word that best describes this film is necessary. It's simply necessary. Some of the commentary is on the nose, but that's the point. People pointing that out like it's some sort of insightful revelation puzzle me. We as a society are on the nose. We've jumped the shark, and movies like this and the Idiocracy are no longer ham-fisted they're just honest.

We are all overly obsessed with our screens (myself included), and it's contributed to the eroding of the social fabric. It just point blank has, and it's not being "anti technology" to point this out and say we should do something about it.

When we're at a point where A-list movie stars are telling us that they're having to make Netflix movies where they're required to re-state the plot three or four times with expository dialogue because people can't go 90 minutes without mindlessly scrolling their phones, then we've got a problem. And a movie like this gives me hope that maybe, just maybe, there are enough people out there that are ready to say enough is enough and fight back. The revolution begins tonight, indeed.

I watch lots of movies that can be described as weird, unique, different. Most of the time it doesn't work for me. This is a great example of when it does. The weirdness makes it that much more of memorable experience.

Imagine taking multiple episodes of Black Mirror and tying them all together in a cohesive narrative. Then make it bigger and more cinematic. Add some hysterical dark humor (the clumsy joke had me dying). And throw in some outrageous style and haunting imagery.

If that sounds interesting to you, go watch this ASAP. I went in knowing nothing about it and I had a blast. I'm glad to see beast Sam Rockwell given a lead role in a great movie. He's such a good actor and doesn't get enough respect.

(1 viewing, early screening Mystery Movie Monday 1/26/2026)

Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die feels like a mix of a dystopian tech satire, a slightly unhinged road movie and an almost cartoonish comedy.

The first act in particular promises this big, chaotic adventure through a collapsing digital nightmare. However, as the plot develops it becomes a lot of running from place to place instead - all while a lot of cryptic exposition gets dropped.

The biggest reason it works as well as it does is Sam Rockwell, who is just an absolute joy to watch. Without him, this probably dips much lower.

Overall, it's not bad. It's just frustratingly close to being better. There's a clever movie buried in here somewhere, but the execution feels a bit too messy and a little self-indulgent.

Basically feels like a few episodes of Black Mirror tied together with a theme running through it.

Surprised no one else is mentioning it. Surprised Netflix didn't snap it up. Surprised it got Gore Verbinski and a cinema release. Keep it up.

Hopefully the masses will understand the meaning and references.
